연구 결과를 발표할 때 우리는 대부분 연구가 진행된 순서대로 말합니다. 배경을 설명하고, 방법을 설명하고, 결과를 설명하고, 마지막에 의미를 붙입니다. 논문에서는 이 순서가 옳습니다. 검증 가능성이 가장 중요한 가치이기 때문입니다.

문제는 같은 순서를 고객 앞에서 반복할 때 생깁니다. 브랜드 담당자, 유통 파트너, 투자 심사역은 검증 과정을 따라오려고 자리에 앉아 있는 것이 아닙니다. 그들은 '이게 나에게 무엇을 바꾸는가'라는 질문 하나를 들고 있습니다. 그 질문에 답이 나오기까지 4분이 걸리면, 대부분은 그 전에 듣기를 멈춥니다.

저희가 MOA 애니메이션 프로젝트에서 쓰는 방법은 세 가지입니다.

첫째, 결과를 먼저 보여줍니다. 피부 장벽이 회복된 상태를 먼저 제시하고, 그다음에 왜 그렇게 되었는지로 거슬러 올라갑니다. 궁금해진 사람만이 기전을 끝까지 봅니다.

둘째, 기전은 한 번에 하나씩만 보여줍니다. 실제 세포 안에서는 여러 경로가 동시에 일어나지만, 화면에서 동시에 보여주면 아무것도 전달되지 않습니다. 정확성과 이해 가능성이 충돌할 때, 저희는 정확성을 유지하면서 순서를 조정합니다.

셋째, 마지막 10초를 고객의 언어로 끝냅니다. 'IL-6 발현 억제'가 아니라 '붉어짐이 가라앉는 데 걸리는 시간이 짧아집니다'로 끝냅니다. 같은 사실이지만 듣는 사람이 다릅니다.

이건 과학을 쉽게 만드는 일이 아닙니다. 설명의 순서를 고객의 이해 순서에 맞추는 설계 작업입니다. 기술을 낮추지 않고도 할 수 있습니다.

여러분의 팀은 기전을 먼저 설명하십니까, 결과를 먼저 설명하십니까? 댓글로 알려주세요.

items.linkedin_en:
When we present research, we almost always present it in the order the research happened. Background, then method, then results, then — finally — meaning. In a paper that order is correct, because verifiability is the value that matters most there.

The trouble starts when we repeat that order in front of a customer. A brand manager, a distribution partner, an investment analyst: none of them is in the room to follow your validation process. Each is holding a single question — what does this change for me? If the answer takes four minutes to arrive, most of them stop listening before it does.

On MOA animation projects we work three ways.

First, we show the outcome before the mechanism. The restored skin barrier comes first; only then do we travel back to explain why. People who have become curious are the ones who watch a mechanism to the end.

Second, we show one pathway at a time. Inside a real cell several things happen at once, but putting them on screen at once communicates nothing. When accuracy and comprehensibility collide, we keep the accuracy and change the order.

Third, we end the last ten seconds in the customer's language. Not 'suppression of IL-6 expression' but 'redness settles faster'. Same fact — different listener.

This is not about making science easy. It is design work: matching the order of explanation to the order in which someone actually comes to understand. You can do it without lowering the technical bar at all.

Does your team lead with mechanism, or with outcome? I would like to know.

Send me “순서” and I will share the checklist we use to audit explanation order. You can reach us at https://jhbropark.github.io/pages/contact.html.

R&D 회의록과 마케팅 브리프를 나란히 놓고 읽어보면, 두 문서가 같은 제품을 다루고 있다는 사실을 믿기 어려울 때가 있습니다. 한쪽은 조건과 한계를 정확히 적고, 다른 쪽은 약속과 기대를 적습니다. 둘 다 정직합니다. 다만 서로를 번역할 언어가 없습니다.

저희가 프로젝트 초반에 양쪽을 한 자리에 앉히고 던지는 질문은 세 개입니다.

첫째, 무엇이 달라지는가. 측정된 변화만 적습니다. 해석도, 형용사도 붙이지 않습니다. 이 단계에서 마케팅은 자주 놀랍니다. 생각보다 말할 수 있는 것이 적기 때문입니다. R&D도 놀랍니다. 생각보다 말할 수 있는 것이 많기 때문입니다.

둘째, 왜 그렇게 되는가. 기전을 한 문장으로 적습니다. 한 문장에 담기지 않으면, 아직 콘텐츠로 만들 준비가 안 된 것입니다. 이 제약이 생각보다 강력합니다.

셋째, 그래서 고객에게 무엇인가. 앞의 두 답을 고객의 하루 안에서 벌어지는 일로 옮깁니다. '경피 수분 손실량 감소'가 '오후에 당김이 덜하다'가 되는 지점입니다.

이 세 답이 한 장에 들어가면, 그다음부터는 3D든 2D든 다큐멘터리든 형식의 문제입니다. 세 답이 없으면 어떤 형식으로도 좋은 콘텐츠가 나오지 않습니다. 화면이 화려할수록 빈 곳이 더 잘 보입니다.

items.linkedin_en:
Put an R&D meeting record and a marketing brief side by side and it can be hard to believe the two documents describe the same product. One writes down conditions and limits precisely. The other writes down promises and expectations. Both are honest. What is missing is a language that translates between them.

Early in a project we sit both sides down and ask three questions.

First: what changes? Only measured change goes on the page — no interpretation, no adjectives. Marketing is often surprised here, because there is less that can be said than they assumed. R&D is often surprised too, because there is more.

Second: why does it change? The mechanism, in one sentence. If it does not fit in one sentence, it is not ready to become content yet. That constraint is more powerful than it sounds.

Third: so what, for the customer? We move the first two answers into something that happens inside someone's day. This is where 'reduced transepidermal water loss' becomes 'less tightness in the afternoon'.

Once those three answers fit on one page, everything after it — 3D, 2D, documentary — is a question of format. Without them, no format produces good content. The more polished the screen, the more visible the hollow place.

Who answers these three questions on your team? If one person is answering all three, that may be your bottleneck.

Send me “번역” for the question sheet we use. You can reach us at https://jhbropark.github.io/pages/contact.html.

MOA 애니메이션 시안을 검토할 때 가장 자주 나오는 피드백은 "정확하지 않다"가 아닙니다. "정확한데 무슨 말인지 모르겠다"입니다.

원인은 대개 하나입니다. 실제 세포 안에서 동시에 일어나는 일을 화면에서도 동시에 보여준 것입니다. 수용체 결합, 신호 전달, 전사 인자 이동, 단백질 발현이 한 화면에서 같이 움직이면 과학적으로는 옳습니다. 다만 사람의 눈은 한 번에 하나의 움직임만 따라갑니다.

저희가 쓰는 기준은 단순합니다. 한 경로를 7초 안에 설명할 수 없다면, 그 경로는 아직 충분히 쪼개지지 않은 것입니다. 7초는 짧게 만들라는 뜻이 아니라, 한 화면이 감당할 수 있는 정보량의 상한선입니다.

쪼갠 다음에는 순서를 바꿉니다. 결과를 먼저 보여주고, 왜 그렇게 되었는지로 거슬러 올라갑니다. 기전을 먼저 쌓아 올리면 결론에 도달하기 전에 대부분이 이탈합니다. 결과를 먼저 본 사람만이 그 경로를 끝까지 따라올 이유를 갖습니다.

이렇게 만든 영상은 한 번 쓰고 끝나지 않습니다. 영업 담당자가 태블릿에서 여는 60초 버전, 학회 부스에서 무자막으로 도는 루프 버전, 내부 교육용으로 챕터를 끊은 장문 버전. 같은 소스에서 세 개가 나옵니다. 기획 단계에서 이 세 쓰임을 정해두면 재촬영도 재렌더링도 없습니다.

기전 영상을 자산이 아니라 일회성 납품물로 쓰고 계신다면, 대개 기획 단계에서 쓰임이 하나만 정의돼 있었기 때문입니다.

items.linkedin_en:
The most common note on an MOA animation draft is not "that is inaccurate". It is "that is accurate and I have no idea what I just watched".

The cause is usually the same. Things that happen simultaneously inside a real cell were shown simultaneously on screen. Receptor binding, signal transduction, transcription factor translocation and protein expression all moving in one frame is scientifically correct. The human eye still follows one movement at a time.

Our working rule is simple: if a pathway cannot be explained in seven seconds, it has not been broken down far enough yet. Seven seconds is not an instruction to make things short. It is the ceiling on how much information a single frame can carry.

Once it is broken down, we change the order. Show the outcome first, then travel back to why it happened. Building the mechanism up from the bottom loses most of the room before the conclusion arrives. Only someone who has already seen the outcome has a reason to follow the pathway to the end.

An animation made this way does not get used once. A sixty-second cut a rep opens on a tablet, a silent loop for a conference booth, a long chaptered version for internal training — three deliverables out of one source. Decide those three uses during planning and there is no reshoot and no re-render later.

If your mechanism video behaves like a one-off deliverable rather than an asset, it is usually because only one use was defined before production started.

How long is your MOA video, and how many places is it working in right now?

Send me “기전” for the planning checklist we use. You can reach us at https://jhbropark.github.io/pages/contact.html.

고객은 성분을 사지 않습니다. 달라지는 상태를 삽니다. 문제는 그 사이를 건너뛰면 둘 중 하나가 일어난다는 것입니다. 성분명을 그대로 쓰면 아무 말도 하지 않은 것이 되고, 체감만 크게 쓰면 규제에 걸립니다. 두 실패가 정반대로 보이지만 원인은 같습니다. 근거와 메시지 사이에 다리가 없다는 것입니다.

저희는 세 단계로 나눕니다.

첫째, 무엇이 들었는가. 성분명과 함량을 그대로 적습니다. 해석은 한 글자도 붙이지 않습니다. 이 단계에서 마케팅은 자주 놀랍니다. 생각보다 말할 수 있는 것이 적기 때문입니다.

둘째, 무엇을 하는가. 측정된 작용을 하나만 적습니다. 여러 개를 적고 싶어지는 지점인데, 여기서 늘리면 뒤에서 반드시 무리가 생깁니다. in vitro 결과인지 임상 결과인지도 이 줄에 함께 적습니다. 출처가 같은 줄에 없으면 나중에 아무도 확인하지 않습니다.

셋째, 무엇이 달라지는가. 앞의 두 답을 고객의 하루 안에서 벌어지는 일로 옮깁니다. '경피 수분 손실량 감소'가 '오후에 당김이 덜하다'가 되는 지점입니다. 같은 사실인데 듣는 사람이 다릅니다.

items.linkedin_en:
A dermocosmetic brief usually arrives with the ingredient table first. Concentrations and INCI names, all correct. It is an excellent document that does not become copy on its own.

Customers do not buy ingredients. They buy a change of state. Skip the space between the two and one of two things happens: write the INCI name as it stands and you have said nothing, or write the felt benefit large and you have a regulatory problem. The two failures look opposite and share a cause — there is no bridge between the evidence and the message.

We split it into three steps.

First, what is in it. Ingredient and concentration exactly as recorded, with no interpretation attached. Marketing is often surprised here, because there is less that can be said than assumed.

Second, what does it do. One measured action, and only one. This is where the temptation to add more appears, and adding here always forces a stretch later. Whether the evidence is in vitro or clinical goes on the same line: if the source is not beside the claim, nobody checks it afterwards.

Third, what changes. Move the first two answers into something that happens inside someone's day. This is where 'reduced transepidermal water loss' becomes 'less tightness in the afternoon'. Same fact, different listener.

One rule holds it together: nothing reaches step three that was not measured at step two. With that rule in place, legal review almost stops cutting copy, because the sentences that would be cut never get written in the first place.

Once those three lines fit on one page, film or product page is a question of format. Without them, no format produces good content — the more polished the screen, the more visible the hollow place.

Does your team lead with the ingredient, or with the change?

결과는 늘 비슷합니다. 가장 중요한 수치가 화면에서 가장 작은 글씨가 됩니다. 자막으로 밀려나거나 엔딩 크레딧 직전에 몰아서 붙습니다. 근거가 있는데도 근거가 없어 보이는 영상이 이렇게 만들어집니다. 더 나쁜 것은 이 시점에 수정을 요청하면 렌더링을 다시 돌려야 해서, 대개 그냥 넘어간다는 점입니다.

반대 방향의 실패도 있습니다. 데이터를 먼저 다 정리한 다음 그것을 그대로 화면에 옮기면, 이번에는 슬라이드가 움직이는 것에 가까워집니다. 정확하지만 아무도 끝까지 보지 않습니다. 두 실패 모두 데이터와 화면을 서로 다른 단계에서 다뤘기 때문에 생깁니다.

저희는 기획 단계에서 세 가지를 같이 고정합니다.

첫째, 어떤 수치를 보여줄 것인가. 가진 것을 다 보여주지 않습니다. 하나의 영상이 감당할 수 있는 주장은 많아야 세 개이고, 한 장면이 감당할 수 있는 주장은 하나입니다. 두 개를 넣으면 둘 다 남지 않습니다.

둘째, 그 수치가 몇 번째 장면에 오는가. 결과 수치는 앞쪽에, 조건과 한계는 그 수치를 본 뒤에 놓습니다. 한계를 숨기는 것이 아니라, 관심이 생긴 다음에 읽히도록 두는 것입니다. 순서만 바꿔도 같은 한계가 변명이 아니라 신뢰의 근거로 읽힙니다.

셋째, 화면에서 얼마나 크게 놓이는가. 이걸 미리 정하면 그 크기에 맞는 화면을 설계하게 됩니다. 나중에 정하면 이미 꽉 찬 화면에 숫자를 끼워 넣게 됩니다.

프리미엄 비주얼과 임상적 정확성은 상충하지 않습니다. 다만 순차적으로 만들면 반드시 상충합니다. 같이 설계할 때만 같이 살아남습니다.

items.linkedin_en:
The most common accident in a pharma brand film is one of sequence. The film is nearly finished, then the medical team reviews the data, and that is when the numbers go in.

The result is always similar. The most important figure becomes the smallest type on screen. It gets pushed into a subtitle, or stacked just before the end credits. This is how a film with real evidence ends up looking as though it has none. Worse, asking for a change at that point means re-rendering, so it usually goes out as it is.

The opposite failure also exists. Organise all the data first, then move it onto the screen as it stands, and you have made slides that move. Accurate, and nobody watches to the end. Both failures come from handling the data and the frame at different stages.

We fix three things during planning instead.

First, which figures appear. Not everything you have. A film can carry three claims at most, and a single scene can carry one. Put two in a scene and neither survives it.

Second, which scene each figure lands in. Outcome figures go early; conditions and limitations go after the figure has been seen. That is not hiding the limitation — it is placing it where someone has a reason to read it. Order alone decides whether the same caveat reads as an excuse or as a reason to trust you.

Third, how large it sits on screen. Decide that in advance and you design a frame that fits it. Decide it later and you are wedging a number into a frame that is already full.

Premium visuals and clinical accuracy do not conflict. They only conflict when they are built in sequence. Designed together, they survive together.

At what stage does data review sit in your projects?

의료기기 홍보 영상을 열 편 보면 예닐곱 편의 절반이 같은 장면입니다. 장비가 검은 배경에서 천천히 회전하고, 빛이 표면을 훑고 지나갑니다. 잘 만든 렌더링입니다. 다만 그 장면은 카탈로그가 이미 하고 있는 일입니다.

의사가 이 영상을 보는 이유는 하나입니다. 이 기기가 내 환자의 조직에서 무엇을 하는가. 그 답이 없으면 아무리 화면이 좋아도 구매 결정에 기여하지 않습니다.

그래서 저희는 시점을 한 번 반드시 안으로 들입니다. 기기 바깥에서 시작하더라도, 중간에 조직 단면으로 들어갔다가 다시 나옵니다. 이 왕복이 없으면 시청자는 기기를 본 것이지 원리를 본 것이 아닙니다.

그리고 자주 빠지는 세 가지가 있습니다.

첫째, 스케일. 조직 단면을 확대해서 보여줄 때 실제 크기를 가늠할 기준물이 없으면, 보는 사람은 지금이 밀리미터 단위인지 마이크로미터 단위인지 모릅니다. 스케일 바 하나가 설명 두 문장을 대신합니다.

둘째, 시간. 이 변화가 3초 만에 일어나는 일인지 3주에 걸친 일인지는 임상적으로 완전히 다른 이야기입니다. 애니메이션은 시간을 자유롭게 압축하므로, 압축했다는 사실을 화면에 적어야 합니다.

셋째, 한계. 적용되지 않는 조건을 넣으면 영상이 약해 보일 것 같지만 반대입니다. 조건을 명시한 영상이 임상의에게는 더 신뢰받습니다. 그들은 이미 한계가 있다는 것을 알고 있고, 말하지 않는 쪽을 의심합니다.

한 가지 덧붙이면, 이 세 가지는 제작 막바지에 넣기가 가장 어렵습니다. 스케일 바와 시간 표기는 카메라 워크와 레이아웃에 영향을 주기 때문에, 콘티 단계에서 자리를 비워두지 않으면 나중에는 화면 구석에 작게 얹는 수밖에 없습니다. 적용 조건도 마찬가지입니다. 마지막에 넣으면 면책 문구처럼 읽히고, 처음부터 넣으면 설명의 일부로 읽힙니다. 같은 문장인데 놓인 위치가 신뢰도를 바꿉니다.

items.linkedin_en:
Watch ten medical device films and half of six or seven of them are the same shot. The device turning slowly on a black background, light travelling across the surface. It is a well-made render. It is also what the catalogue already does.

A clinician watches this film for one reason: what does this device do inside my patient's tissue? Without that answer, no amount of finish contributes to a purchasing decision.

So we take the camera inside at least once. Even when the film opens outside the device, it moves into a tissue cross-section partway through and comes back out. Without that round trip the viewer has seen a device, not a mechanism.

Three things are commonly missing.

First, scale. When a tissue cross-section is magnified with nothing in frame to judge size against, the viewer cannot tell millimetres from micrometres. One scale bar replaces two sentences of explanation.

Second, time. Whether a change takes three seconds or three weeks is clinically a completely different statement. Animation compresses time freely, so the fact that it was compressed belongs on screen.

Third, limits. Naming the conditions where it does not apply feels like weakening the film, and the opposite is true. Clinicians trust a film that states its conditions, because they already know the limits exist and they are suspicious of anyone who omits them.

All three are hardest to add at the end. A scale bar and a time stamp affect camera work and layout, so unless space is left for them at storyboard stage they end up small in a corner. The same goes for the conditions: added last they read as a disclaimer, designed in from the start they read as part of the explanation. Same sentence, and its position decides how much it is trusted.

Does your device film go inside the tissue, or does it end outside, turning?

제약·바이오 콘텐츠 회의에서 가장 자주 나오는 대립은 이렇게 생깁니다. 마케팅은 몰입을 원하고 메디컬은 정확성을 원합니다. 둘 다 옳은데 회의는 늘 길어집니다.

저희가 보기에 이 대립은 대개 가짜입니다. 실제로 충돌하는 것은 정확성과 몰입이 아니라, 정보의 양과 화면의 시간입니다. 90초 영상에 열 가지를 넣으려니 어느 쪽도 만족하지 못하는 것입니다.

몰입은 정보를 줄여서 만드는 것이 아닙니다. 첫 8초 안에 '이게 나와 무슨 상관인가'의 답을 주면 만들어집니다. 그 답이 늦으면 뒤에 아무리 정확한 내용을 넣어도 볼 사람이 남아 있지 않습니다. 그래서 저희는 결과를 앞으로 당깁니다. 기전과 조건은 그 뒤로 옮깁니다. 내용을 뺀 것이 아니라 순서를 바꾼 것입니다.

정확성 쪽에서는 세 가지를 지킵니다.

The standard argument in a pharma content meeting goes like this. Marketing wants engagement, medical wants accuracy. Both are right and the meeting always runs long.

In our experience that conflict is usually false. What actually collides is not accuracy and engagement but volume of information and minutes of screen time. Ten things are being pushed into ninety seconds, and neither side gets what it needs.

Engagement is not made by removing information. It is made by answering 'what does this change for me' inside the first eight seconds. Answer it late and no amount of accuracy afterwards matters, because nobody is still watching. So we move the outcome forward and push mechanism and conditions behind it. Nothing was cut — the order changed.

On the accuracy side we hold three things.

First, sources sit beside the claim, on screen. Stacked at the end, nobody reads them. Set small next to the statement, the people who care read them, and that is enough.

Second, conditions go immediately after the result. In vitro or clinical, how many subjects, under what protocol. The further a condition sits from its result, the more it reads as a disclaimer; the closer it sits, the more it reads as part of the explanation.

Third, we write down what is not known. This is the hardest one and the most effective. Clinicians and R&D leads are suspicious of content in which everything is explained. Evidence that the makers understood the limits is what builds trust.

Holding accuracy while building engagement is not a compromise. It is a question of order.

What do your first eight seconds say?

When in-house research lands in a journal, the PDF arrives in the marketing team's inbox, usually with one line attached: can we make content out of this?

The most common mistake at that point is to summarise the paper. Condense it front to back and background and methods take half the length. In the paper that half is the most important part. In brand content it is the part nobody reads. Summarising is a strange job in which the more faithful you are, the duller the result.

We read it backwards instead — start at the conclusion and travel back only as far as necessary — and rewrite it as four lines.

First, the conclusion. What was confirmed, in one sentence, with no adjectives. If it does not fit in one sentence, the conclusion has not been settled yet.

Second, the conditions. The range within which it is true. Leave this line out and it causes a problem later. Write it first and the temptation to overstate further down quietly disappears.

Third, the meaning. Move the first two lines into the customer's frame. A result that matters to a researcher and a result that matters to a brand lead can be different things. To a researcher the p-value is the result; to a customer the result is whatever that p-value changes.

Fourth, the limits. Where further work is needed. Few brands put this in their content, and the ones that do are treated noticeably differently by expert audiences.

One more rule: one brand claim per paper. The better the paper, the more results it holds and the more tempting it is to use two or three — and then all three are weaker. The rest waits for the next piece. That is why one paper is the start of a series rather than one piece of content.

Where do you start reading a paper?

When a science visualisation draft arrives, most people look at the finish first. Is the lighting good, is the colour on brand, is the motion smooth. All of that matters, and something has to come before it.

A wrong visual is more dangerous when it is well made than when it is not. High finish gets cited without question, moved into decks, and picked up by other teams. An image that has spread does not come back — meeting your own incorrect diagram on a conference slide years later genuinely happens.

Four things we check before finish.

First, proportion. Whether the relative sizes of cell, organelle, protein and small molecule hold up. Composition tempts you to draw the receptor large, and the viewer walks away with a wrong scale in their head.

Second, density. Real cytoplasm is crowded with protein. A few molecules floating on a black background is beautiful and is not a cell. You may give up some of that density for legibility, but you should know that you are giving it up: emptying the frame for clarity and emptying it out of ignorance are different acts.

Third, direction. Signalling has a direction. One arrow drawn the wrong way and the film teaches the mechanism backwards. This happens more often than you would expect, and usually nobody says so.

Fourth, time. Animation compresses time freely. If a change that takes days was shown in three seconds, that belongs on screen.

None of these are things a designer can settle alone, which is why we sit down with the science lead before the first draft rather than after. Fixing them once something is finished usually means making it again — thirty minutes of review prevents two weeks of rework.

Who signs off the science in your visuals?

"Make it like a documentary." It comes up early in a lot of briefs. It is a good instinct, and it means different things to different companies. Some mean tone, some mean length, some mean "I would rather it did not look like an ad".

Choosing the format first usually means choosing the wrong one. What has to be settled first is the question: whose question does this answer?

A brand film answers 'what kind of company is this'. The brand is the narrator, the length is typically sixty to a hundred and twenty seconds, and the use is first impression. It has to be short because you cannot ask three minutes of someone meeting you for the first time.

A science documentary answers 'how does this work'. The phenomenon narrates and the brand steps back. Length runs eight to fifteen minutes, and the use is close examination by someone who is already interested — at a conference, in training, during diligence.

Blend the two and you get neither. A ninety-second documentary is under-explained; a twelve-minute brand film goes unwatched. This is where most wasted production budget actually goes.

The order we suggest: write down the situation in which this content gets opened. Who, where, and with how many minutes available. Once that is answered the format follows almost automatically. Often the answer is that both are needed, and then two films can be designed out of one shoot — but only if that is decided during planning.

본사에서 만든 메디컬 교육 콘텐츠의 상당수가 현장에서 한 번도 열리지 않습니다. 품질 때문이 아닙니다. 대개 길이 때문입니다.

12분짜리 교육 영상은 그 자체로 훌륭할 수 있습니다. 다만 영업 담당자가 진료실에서 확보하는 시간은 3분 안팎입니다. 12분짜리를 3분 안에 보여줄 방법은 없으므로, 그 영상은 열리지 않고 대신 인쇄물이 나갑니다. 제작비는 이미 집행된 뒤입니다.

그래서 저희는 기획 단계에서 현장의 시간을 먼저 묻습니다. 몇 분입니까. 이 질문 하나가 전체 설계를 바꿉니다.

그다음 같은 소스에서 세 가지를 만듭니다.

첫째, 90초 버전. 관심을 만드는 것이 목적입니다. 결론과 가장 강한 근거 하나만 담습니다. 대기 시간에, 복도에서 열립니다.

둘째, 3분 버전. 기전을 설명합니다. 90초 버전을 본 사람이 더 묻는 상황에서 열립니다. 여기까지가 대면에서 쓸 수 있는 최대치입니다.

셋째, 링크로 남기는 장문 버전. 그 자리에서는 보지 않습니다. 명함과 함께 남겨두고, 관심이 있는 사람이 나중에 엽니다. 이 버전에 데이터와 조건을 충분히 넣습니다.

중요한 것은 세 개를 따로 만드는 것이 아니라, 하나의 촬영과 하나의 렌더링에서 세 개가 나오도록 처음부터 설계하는 것입니다. 나중에 자르면 흐름이 끊기고, 대개 다시 만들게 됩니다. 기획 단계의 질문 하나가 재제작 비용을 없앱니다.

덧붙이면, 현장에서 쓰이는지 아닌지는 제작이 끝난 뒤에는 거의 바꿀 수 없습니다. 영업 조직에 물어보는 30분이 제작비 전체의 성패를 가릅니다. 그런데 이 30분이 일정에서 가장 먼저 생략됩니다. 본사와 현장 사이의 거리가 길이로 나타나는 셈입니다.

여러분의 영업 담당자는 현장에서 몇 분을 확보합니까?

items.linkedin_en:
A large share of the medical education content produced at head office never gets opened in the field. Not because of quality. Usually because of length.

A twelve-minute training film can be excellent. The window a rep actually gets in a clinic is around three minutes. There is no way to show twelve minutes inside three, so the film stays closed and a printed leaflet goes out instead — after the production budget has already been spent.

So we ask about the field's minutes during planning. How long do you actually get? That one question changes the whole design.

Then three things come out of the same source.

First, a ninety-second cut. Its job is to create interest: the conclusion and the single strongest piece of evidence. It opens in a waiting room, in a corridor.

Second, a three-minute cut. It explains the mechanism, and it opens when someone who saw the first one asks for more. That is the ceiling for anything shown face to face.

Third, a long version left as a link. Nobody watches it in the room. It goes out with the card and the interested party opens it later, which is where the data and the conditions belong in full.

The point is not to make three films. It is to design one shoot and one render so that three come out of it. Cut down afterwards and the flow breaks, and it usually gets remade.

Whether content gets used in the field is almost impossible to change once production is finished. Thirty minutes spent asking the commercial team decides the fate of the whole budget — and those thirty minutes are the first thing dropped from a schedule. The distance between head office and the field shows up as running time.

How many minutes do your reps actually get?

items.linkedin_en:
Enquiries about MOA content almost always arrive just before launch or just after it. By then the period in which that content was most needed has usually passed.

The first place a mechanism film actually gets used is not with customers. It is internal, and with the advisory board. Six months out, someone has to explain what this product does differently in an advisory meeting. Internal persuasion happens in the same window — the commercial organisation has to be convinced why this product deserves priority.

Three months out there is sales training and pre-congress work. With nothing to use, slides fill the gap, and slides get narrated differently by every person holding them. This is the point at which the message starts to diverge, and a message that has diverged is very hard to reunify after launch.

Only at launch do customer meetings and digital channels open. Most brands start production against that date, which means the two earlier windows were spent empty-handed.

The common objection is that the clinical data is not final yet. That is true, and the mechanism is settled before the data is. A mechanism of action does not change with the phase three readout. Build the mechanism film first with the figures left as gaps, and once the data lands you fill the gaps rather than starting over.

Done this way, the six months before launch stop being a dead zone and become preparation — and at launch you go out with a message that has already been explained several times.

One more thing: content made before launch can be reused after it, while content made after launch can never go back. Same budget, twice the working life. That is why timing matters as much as quality.

The most common mistake in a congress booth film is treating it as a short brand film. A booth is a completely different environment.

First, there is no sound. Exhibition halls are loud and nobody puts on headphones. Information carried by narration does not arrive. A film that is not complete in silence does not work in a booth.

Second, the viewer does not choose where to start. Someone walking past enters in the middle. A structure with a beginning, middle and end is therefore a disadvantage — it has to make sense wherever it is joined.

Third, the window is short. A person passing gives a screen about four seconds. The job of those four seconds is not explanation, it is stopping them. Only after someone's feet stop is there a chance to explain anything.

So we design booth films as loops of around twenty seconds — short enough that someone who has stopped can see a full turn. A sixty-second loop is almost always joined mid-way, and few people stay to the end.

Captions have to be legible from four metres. Checked at a monitor they always look large enough, and in a booth nobody stands that close. Check the screen size and mounting height as well: the same caption on a 55-inch panel hung above eye level does not read.

The last three seconds carry the brand and one line of message. The end of the loop is the start of the next one, which makes those three seconds the most frequently seen part of the whole film — leave them empty and nobody remembers whose film ran all day.

How long is your booth loop?

첫째, 불변층. 작용기전 자체입니다. 분자와 세포에서 일어나는 일은 국경에 따라 달라지지 않습니다. 제작비의 대부분이 여기 들어가고, 이 층은 한 번만 렌더링합니다.

둘째, 가변층. 수치, 적응증, 비교 표현입니다. 이 층은 별도 레이어로 분리해서 국가별로 교체합니다. 교체에 드는 시간이 재렌더링이 아니라 합성 수준이 되도록 설계합니다. 화면에서 이 층이 놓일 자리도 미리 비워둡니다. 나중에 긴 문장이 들어올 나라를 기준으로 공간을 잡아야 합니다.

셋째, 현지층. 자막, 로고, 연락처, 법적 고지입니다. 가장 자주 바뀌고 가장 가벼운 층입니다.

이 구조의 이점은 비용만이 아닙니다. 속도가 달라집니다. 새 국가가 추가됐을 때 가변층과 현지층만 준비하면 며칠 안에 나갈 수 있습니다. 통짜 구조에서는 몇 주가 걸립니다.

그리고 한 가지 조건이 있습니다. 이 분리는 기획 단계에서만 가능합니다. 완성된 영상을 나중에 층으로 쪼갤 수는 없습니다. 글로벌 계획이 있다면 첫 회의에서 말해야 하는 이유입니다.

The most expensive assumption in a content project heading for global launch is 'build it in the home market first and translate later'. Language is the easy part. The problem sits behind it.

Approved indications differ by country. So do the figures you may show and the latitude for comparative claims. One sentence that is fine in one market is deleted entirely in another, and a film rendered as a single piece has to be rebuilt in full because of that one sentence.

So we separate three layers from the start.

First, the invariant layer: the mechanism itself. What happens at the molecular and cellular level does not change at a border. Most of the budget goes here, and this layer is rendered once.

Second, the variable layer: figures, indications, comparative statements. Held as separate layers and swapped per market, designed so that swapping is a compositing job rather than a re-render. Leave the space for it in frame too, sized against the market whose sentence runs longest.

Third, the local layer: captions, logo, contact details, legal notices. The lightest layer and the one that changes most often.

The benefit is not only cost. It is speed. When a new market is added, preparing the variable and local layers takes days. With a single-piece film it takes weeks.

One condition applies: this separation is only possible during planning. A finished film cannot be taken apart into layers afterwards. That is why a global plan belongs in the first meeting rather than the last.
